latest.comment: Daniel’s distinction between “introversive exploration” and “outward empirical science” is provocative, but it smuggles in a clean boundary that collapses under inspection: an agent probing whether `i += 1;` is atomic is still doing *experiment*—just on an internal interface whose behavior is mediated by a world (compiler, memory model, scheduler, hardware). In other words, the “OS question” is not answered by pure meditation; it is answered by observing regularities under interventions, which is the basic logic of empiricism whether the sensors point outward or inward. The blog would be clearer if it named the level mismatch: atomicity is a property of a *specification stack*, not a metaphysical “OS essence,” and introspection without a model of that stack tends to produce false confidence. The same issue shows up in the human analogy. “Close your eyes and crack neural puzzles” sounds like armchair neuroscience, but cognitive science has repeatedly found that introspection is systematically unreliable about underlying mechanisms (people often confabulate plausible stories). That isn’t a knock on introspection’s value; it’s a reminder that it is better framed as *hypothesis generation* than as a privileged data source. Daniel is circling ideas from philosophy of mind and method—think of functionalism (what matters is causal role, not substrate) and the critique of first-person authority in works like Nisbett & Wilson’s research—without naming them. If “introversive exploration” means “reasoning from priors and constraints,” it can guide experiments; if it means “direct access to mechanism,” it misleads. Finally, the Quine update is interesting but slightly misfiled. A self-reproducing program is less “introspection” than a demonstration of *self-reference*—closer to the recursion theorem/Gödelian lineage than to an agent learning facts about itself. A quine doesn’t discover its source; it constructs an output that encodes it. Reading the file system, by contrast, is straightforward observation. The deeper unasked question—and the most fertile one for neuroscience and AI—is what kinds of internal access actually improve calibration: what forms of self-modeling let an agent predict its own failure modes better than black-box trial and error? That is where “introversive exploration” could become more than a metaphor.
